strengths: Addresses a practically important failure mode: personalized subjects can overwhelm contextual instructions. Training trajectories, embedding analyses, and qualitative examples provide useful evidence of this behavior.

The proposed norm adjustment and spherical interpolation are simple, inexpensive, and require no additional training. Experiments demonstrate applicability to Textual Inversion, DreamBooth, and Custom Diffusion.

Separating context, subject, and full-prompt alignment is informative. DreamBooth on CC101 shows a promising simultaneous improvement of 1.87 in full-prompt CLIP alignment and 4.57 in CLIP image similarity.
weaknesses: The claimed root cause is not established. Correlations between training duration, embedding drift, and context loss do not isolate unconstrained embedding optimization from overfitting or changes in the denoiser/text encoder. Controlled interventions on norm and direction during training are missing, and the distinction from established personalization–editability tradeoffs remains insufficiently demonstrated.

The semantic-collapse metrics contain substantive problems. Table 5 defines inter-set Mahalanobis distance using only P, without Q, and defines intra-set KL divergence as D_KL(P||P), which is identically zero and cannot measure diversity. Covariance regularization and the representation used for prompt-distance calculations are also unspecified. These issues weaken the central analytical evidence.

The method is a straightforward interpolation toward a generic class embedding, but comparisons against linear interpolation, norm-only and direction-only adjustments, earlier checkpoints, or reduced personalization strength are absent. Consequently, the evaluation does not show that TEA improves the fidelity–alignment frontier rather than merely weakening personalization.

The broad improvement claims exceed the results. TI loses CLIP-I and DINO-I fidelity on both datasets, while Custom Diffusion's context alignment decreases on both. Most full-prompt gains are small, and the main result tables lack uncertainty estimates or significance tests. Human evaluation, face-identity metrics, and direct checks of object/action correctness would better establish practical benefits.

Important reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence: Table 2 reports CelebA DreamBooth changes of +0.64/-2.37 in full-prompt CLIP/CLIP-I, whereas Table 7 reports +1.11/-4.55. Section 5.2 describes alpha=1 as 'no rotation', although Equation 1 makes alpha=1 replace the learned direction entirely with the class direction.

Evaluation and reproducibility are limited: experiments use only SD1.5, nine object concepts, and ten identities. The multi-personalized-concept experiments diagnose failure without quantitatively validating TEA as a remedy. Training duration, main-evaluation sampling details, and token-position alignment for Equation 2 are insufficiently specified, and the promised anonymous repository links are missing.

strengths: Addresses a practically important failure mode: personalized subjects can dominate generation and suppress contextual instructions. Training trajectories and multi-concept examples provide useful illustrations.

The proposed norm adjustment and spherical interpolation are simple, inexpensive, and require no additional training. Their application to TI, DreamBooth LoRA, and Custom Diffusion demonstrates some practical flexibility.

There are measurable benefits in selected settings. On CustomConcept101, DreamBooth gains 1.87 CLIP full-prompt alignment points and 4.57 CLIP image-similarity points. The appendix includes per-concept results, qualitative comparisons, and implementation settings.
weaknesses: The claimed root cause is not established. Correlations between embedding drift, training duration, and contextual suppression do not isolate unconstrained embedding optimization from overfitting, reference-image composition, or denoiser changes. Controlled interventions and comparisons at matched subject fidelity are needed. The distinction from previously recognized personalization/editability trade-offs is also insufficiently demonstrated.

The semantic-collapse measurements contain substantive problems. Table 5 defines the inter-set Mahalanobis statistic using only P, so it cannot measure separation from Q. Its intra-set KL quantity D_KL(P || P) is identically zero and cannot diagnose collapse. The representation aggregation and covariance regularization are insufficiently specified, further weakening the central diagnostic evidence.

The results do not establish a consistent improvement in the personalization–alignment trade-off. Table 2 reports TI full-prompt gains of only 0.64 and 0.57 points alongside CLIP-I losses of 2.34 and 2.41 points. Custom Diffusion's context-only alignment actually decreases on both datasets. Without fidelity-matched comparisons, gains could largely reflect weakening personalization.

Important baselines and ablations are missing: early stopping, linear interpolation toward the class embedding, norm-only and direction-only adjustments, and relevant regularization or editability methods. Consequently, neither the necessity of SLERP nor the advantage over simpler ways to reduce subject dominance is demonstrated.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. Section 5.2 describes alpha = 1 as 'no rotation', whereas Equation 1 makes it complete replacement by the reference direction. For CelebA DreamBooth, Table 2 reports full-prompt/CLIP-I changes of +0.64/-2.37, but Table 7 reports +1.11/-4.55. These discrepancies undermine reproducibility and interpretation.

Evaluation is limited to Stable Diffusion 1.5, nine object concepts, and ten identities, with repetitive human prompts. Main comparative results lack uncertainty estimates, human assessment, and dedicated identity or compositional-success measurements. CLIP/DINO similarity alone does not substantiate claims of improved realism or preserved identity, and multi-concept experiments diagnose the problem without quantitatively validating the remedy.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful settings in Appendix E.3. Repository references end without a URL, and important details such as token correspondence for Equation 2 when prompt tokenizations differ, exact Custom Diffusion adjustment, and the main evaluation sampling protocol are insufficiently specified.

strengths: Addresses an important personalization failure: learned subjects can dominate contextual instructions. Training trajectories and qualitative examples usefully illustrate this behavior in both single- and multi-subject settings.
The proposed norm adjustment and spherical interpolation are simple, require no additional training, and can be applied to existing personalized models.

Experiments cover three personalization methods and 19 concepts. DreamBooth on CC101 provides a concrete positive result: full-prompt CLIP alignment improves by 1.87 points while CLIP-I improves by 4.57.
weaknesses: The claimed root cause is not established. Correlations between embedding drift, training duration, and context suppression do not isolate unconstrained embedding optimization from overfitting or the usual identity–editability trade-off. This is especially problematic for DreamBooth, where the input embedding matrix remains unchanged and other model parameters are trained.

The semantic-collapse measurements contain substantive problems. Table 5 defines inter-set Mahalanobis distance using only P, without Q, and defines intra-set KL divergence as D_KL(P||P), which is identically zero and cannot measure diversity. These definitions undermine the claimed corroboration across four metrics.

The experiments do not demonstrate that TEA improves the identity–prompt trade-off over straightforward alternatives. Missing comparisons include early stopping, linear interpolation toward the class embedding, norm-only and rotation-only adjustments, and reduced personalization strength. The novelty and benefit of SLERP therefore remain insufficiently established.

Improvements are mixed and often accompanied by reduced subject fidelity. TI loses CLIP-I and DINO-I on both datasets; Custom Diffusion's context alignment decreases on both datasets. Small full-prompt CLIP gains alone do not establish better compositional generation. Human evaluation, face-identity metrics, and comparisons at matched identity fidelity would strengthen the evidence.

Important reporting inconsistencies impede verification. Section 5.2 calls alpha=1 'no rotation', although Equation 1 makes it complete replacement by the class direction. Table 2 reports CelebA DreamBooth gains of +0.64/-2.37 in full-prompt CLIP/CLIP-I, whereas Table 7 reports +1.11/-4.55.

Evaluation is restricted to Stable Diffusion 1.5, nine CC101 concepts, and ten human identities, with no uncertainty estimates for the main comparisons or quantitative demonstration that TEA resolves multi-personalized-concept collapse. Reproduction also requires clearer specification of prompt pooling, token alignment for Equation 2, training/checkpoint selection, and the evaluation sampling protocol.

strengths: Addresses an important personalization failure: learned subjects can dominate contextual instructions. Tracking embedding geometry alongside context alignment and reference-image similarity provides a useful empirical perspective.
TEA is simple and requires no additional training. Its normalization and spherical interpolation operations can be applied to both learned token embeddings and contextual prompt representations.

Experiments cover six personalization methods, with additional demonstrations on Flux and relationship personalization. DreamBooth on CC101 shows meaningful improvements in both prompt alignment and reference similarity.
The appendix provides extensive qualitative examples, per-concept results, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, and acknowledges the trade-off between prompt alignment and subject fidelity.
weaknesses: The claimed identification of a root cause exceeds the evidence. Embedding drift, reduced prompt diversity, and declining contextual alignment correlate during training, but these observations do not isolate unconstrained embedding optimization from overfitting or changes elsewhere in the model. This is particularly important for DreamBooth, where the paper acknowledges that the token embedding matrix is unchanged. Controlled interventions are needed to establish causality and distinguish SCP from previously recognized personalization trade-offs.

Several diagnostic metrics are incorrectly or incompletely specified. Table 5 defines the inter-set Mahalanobis statistic using only P, so it cannot measure separation from Q. Its intra-set KL divergence is D_KL(P||P), which is identically zero and cannot measure collapse. Covariance inversion is also unexplained for 200 high-dimensional prompt embeddings. These problems undermine the claimed corroboration across four distance metrics.

The method's incremental contribution is insufficiently established against simpler alternatives. Comparisons with linear interpolation, normalization alone, rotation alone, reduced personalization strength, and earlier training checkpoints are missing or incomplete. The paper therefore does not demonstrate that SLERP-based correction improves the fidelity–alignment frontier beyond simply weakening personalization.

The quantitative evidence is mixed. In Table 1, TI gains only 0.64 full-prompt CLIP points on CC101 while losing 2.34 CLIP-I and 3.81 DINO-I points. Context alignment declines for Custom Diffusion on both datasets and ClassDiffusion on CC101. These outcomes do not support uniformly improved contextual composition or preserved subject fidelity. Human evaluation, identity-specific evaluation for faces, and uncertainty estimates for the main comparisons would strengthen the conclusions.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. DreamBooth on CelebA has improvements of +0.64 CLIP-full and -2.37 CLIP-I in Table 1, versus +1.11 and -4.55 in Table 7. Appendix C.1 describes alpha=1 as 'no rotation,' whereas Equation 1 makes alpha=1 complete replacement by the reference direction. These discrepancies affect interpretation of both effectiveness and ablations.

Generality and reproducibility remain limited. The main evaluation uses nine object concepts and ten identities; Flux is tested on only two subjects and ReVersion on three relationships. Implementation details are insufficient for aligning token positions between differently tokenized prompts in Equation 2 and reproducing the distinct conditioning adjustments across architectures.

The Anti-DreamBooth finding is intriguing but primarily qualitative. Reduced distortion does not establish recovery of the protected person's identity rather than generation of a plausible generic face. Quantitative identity-recovery measurements, explicit attack settings, and comparisons with simpler recovery baselines are needed before asserting a substantive privacy-defense vulnerability.

strengths: Addresses an important personalization failure: subject fidelity can improve while contextual prompt adherence deteriorates. Training trajectories and qualitative examples provide useful evidence of this phenomenon.
TEA is simple and requires no additional training: it rescales embeddings and interpolates their direction toward a class reference.
Experiments cover six personalization methods, with encouraging results in some settings. DreamBooth on CC101 improves both full-prompt alignment and reference-image similarity.
weaknesses: The claimed root cause is not established. Correlations between embedding drift, training duration, and context loss do not isolate unconstrained embedding optimization from overfitting or changes in the denoiser/text encoder. Controlled interventions and comparisons with constrained training are missing, particularly for DreamBooth where the token embedding matrix is unchanged.

The semantic-collapse metrics have substantive mathematical problems. Table 5 defines inter-set Mahalanobis distance using only P, so it cannot measure separation from Q, and defines intra-set KL divergence as D_KL(P||P), which is identically zero. Covariance inversion with 200 high-dimensional prompt embeddings also requires an unspecified regularization or dimensionality-reduction procedure. These issues undermine the claimed corroboration across four metrics.

The evaluation does not establish an improved fidelity–alignment trade-off. Table 1 reports losses of 2.34 CLIP-I and 3.81 DINO-I for TI on CC101, while context alignment decreases for several CD/CL settings. Without matched-fidelity comparisons against weaker personalization, earlier checkpoints, or simple embedding interpolation, gains could reflect dilution of the personalized subject.

Important results and ablation descriptions are inconsistent. For DreamBooth on CelebA, Table 1 reports +0.64 CLIP full-prompt alignment and -2.37 CLIP-I, whereas Table 7 reports +1.11 and -4.55. Section C.1 calls alpha=1 'no rotation', although Equation 1 makes it complete replacement by the reference direction. This prevents reliable interpretation of the scaling ablation.

Novelty and comparative evidence are insufficient. The method combines normalization with standard SLERP, but lacks direct comparisons with linear interpolation, prompt weighting, and systematic normalization-only versus rotation-only variants. The distinction from previously recognized semantic drift and the identity–editability trade-off remains insufficiently demonstrated.

Broad robustness claims exceed the evaluation. Flux is tested on only two subjects and relationship personalization on three relations. Main comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, human evaluation, and identity-specific measurements; CLIP/DINO similarity alone does not establish successful composition or preserved facial identity.

The Anti-DreamBooth conclusion relies primarily on visual examples and embedding drift. Less distorted faces do not establish recovery of protected identity; quantitative identity-recovery evaluation and stronger controls are needed before claiming a meaningful privacy-defense vulnerability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: training durations, main-evaluation sampling details, and token correspondence for prompt-level interpolation are insufficiently specified. In particular, replacing an identifier with a class phrase can change tokenization, making Equation 2's positionwise interpolation ambiguous.

strengths: Addresses an important personalization failure: preserving a subject’s appearance while neglecting contextual instructions. Training trajectories and qualitative examples illustrate this behavior in both single- and multiple-concept settings.
TEA is simple and practically appealing: norm adjustment and spherical interpolation require no additional training and can operate on token embeddings or contextualized prompt embeddings.

Experiments cover six personalization methods, including a Flux-based method and relationship personalization. Some results improve both prompt alignment and reference similarity, particularly DreamBooth on CC101.
weaknesses: The central claim of identifying the root cause is stronger than the evidence. Correlations between training duration, embedding drift, and declining contextual alignment do not isolate unconstrained embedding optimization from overfitting or changes to the text encoder and denoiser. Controlled interventions on norm and direction during training, and comparisons with frozen text encoders, would strengthen the causal argument.

The mathematical definitions supporting the diagnostic analysis contain substantive problems. Table 5 defines inter-set Mahalanobis distance using only P, with no dependence on Q, and defines intra-set KL divergence as D_KL(P||P), which is identically zero. Covariance inversion with 200 high-dimensional embeddings also requires an unspecified regularization or dimensionality-reduction procedure. These issues undermine confidence in the claimed agreement across distance metrics.

The evaluation does not establish improvement beyond the familiar identity–editability trade-off. For TI on CC101, a +0.64 full-prompt CLIP gain accompanies losses of 2.34 CLIP-I and 3.81 DINO-I. Context alignment actually decreases for CD and ClassDiffusion on CC101. Comparisons at matched subject fidelity, with face-recognition metrics and human or compositional evaluations, are needed to substantiate the stronger quality claims.

Baselines and ablations do not adequately establish the contribution of the proposed geometry. Missing comparisons include ordinary linear interpolation, token-strength adjustment, earlier training checkpoints, and systematic norm-only versus direction-only interventions. Appendix C.1 calls alpha=1 'no rotation,' whereas Equation 1 makes this complete replacement of the learned direction by the class direction, leaving the scaling experiment ambiguous.

The reported results are internally inconsistent. Table 1 gives CelebA DreamBooth gains of +0.64 CLIP-T and -2.37 CLIP-I, while Table 7 reports +1.11 and -4.55. Main benchmark tables lack uncertainty estimates, which matters for the small improvements reported for several methods. Generalization to Flux is tested on only two concepts.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, particularly how Equation 2 aligns token positions when personalized and class prompts tokenize differently, and how TEA is applied to the different conditioning representations of the additional architectures. The training-free implementation is plausible, but its precise behavior is insufficiently specified.

The Anti-DreamBooth finding is interesting but remains preliminary. Reduced visual distortion does not establish recovery of the protected identity. Quantitative identity-recovery measurements across subjects, explicit attack settings, and comparisons with simpler recovery baselines are needed before concluding that the defense provides a false sense of security.
